topic: The Inseparable Pair: Connecting Derivatives and Integrals
target_audience: Advanced High School or First-Year University Students

sections.title: Recall: The Tools in our Toolbox
sections.content: A brief 45-second recap of prerequisite knowledge. Define the Derivative as the 'rate of change' (slope) and the Definite Integral as the 'accumulation' (area under the curve). Use a simple graph to show a moving point and the shaded region beneath its path.
sections.example: Visualizing a car's speedometer (derivative) versus the total odometer reading (integral) as the car travels down a straight road.

sections.title: The Bridge: Velocity vs. Displacement
sections.content: Transitioning from definitions to relationships. Explain that if we know how fast an object is changing (derivative), we can find out how much it has moved total (integral). This section introduces the concept that these two operations are 'opposites' in a physical sense.
sections.example: A cheetah (Character: 'Spot') sprints. Its velocity curve is f(t). The area under Spot's velocity curve over 5 seconds is the exact distance Spot has traveled.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function Animation
sections.content: Introduce the 'Area-so-far' function, A(x). Use an animation of a vertical 'sweeping line' moving across a graph. As the line moves right, the area (integral) grows. This section demonstrates that the rate at which this area grows is equal to the height of the function at that point.
sections.example: A 'painting robot' moves across a canvas. The height of the brush changes (f(x)). The total paint used (Area) increases faster when the brush is high and slower when the brush is low.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC)
sections.content: The core mathematical reveal. Formalize the relationship: The derivative of the integral is the original function. Explain that differentiation and integration 'undo' each other, much like addition and subtraction.
sections.example: Equation Visual: d/dx [ ∫ f(t) dt from a to x ] = f(x). Show an animation of a 'mathematical machine' where a function goes in, gets integrated, then differentiated, and comes out unchanged.

sections.title: Calculating with Ease: The Evaluation Theorem
sections.content: The practical application of the relationship. Show how to solve a complex area problem using an 'antiderivative' (F(x)) rather than manual counting. This highlights the efficiency of the relationship.
sections.example: To find the area under f(x)=x² from 0 to 3, we find its 'parent' F(x)=x³/3. Area = F(3) - F(0) = 9. Graphically show the area filling in as the calculation completes.

sections.title: Summary: The Infinite Loop
sections.content: A final 30-second wrap-up. A circular diagram showing a function f(x) turning into a derivative f'(x) in one direction, and turning into an integral ∫f(x) in the other. Reinforce that they are two sides of the same coin.
sections.example: A 'Uroboros' snake or a circular gear system where 'Change' (Derivative) and 'Total' (Integral) are perfectly synchronized gears.
